text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- A third of car repairs are below standard, according to a study of 1,282 cars repairs by insurance company Lansforesakringar.

- A state commission of inquiry has started an investigation into a fatal accident last Friday in which two young boys, aged nine and six, were tipped from a paper recycling bin into a truck and crushed to death.

- The Stockholm bourse rose on Monday in line with other European stock markets, recovering some ground after last week's dive. The crown strengthened against the mark and debt yields fell in renewed confidence over the European economic and monetary union (EMU).

- Managing director of Investor Claes Dahlback will step in as vice chairman in S-E-Banken at the bank's AGM this spring, newspaper sources said. This will put him in the prime position to replace Karl-Erik Sahlberg when he retires next year aged 70.

- Swedish vehicle maker AB Volvo is planning to buy Renault's U.S. truck unit Mack, the newspaper said. This will boost Volvo's market share in the U.S. where it currently has 10 percent and Mack has 8.8 percent.

- U.S. authorities issued a warning over children playing in rubbish and paper bins in 1994 but Sweden did not follow this lead. A state commission is now investigating the death of two young brothers who were crushed to death after being tipped from a bin into a truck that compacts paper for recycling.
- More new companies are being set up in Sweden, with high unemployment and generous bankers behind the trend.

- A proposal to lower wages to give teenagers a shot at industrial jobs is causing controversy in Sweden. The metal workers' union at steel and tool manufacturer Sandvik is ready to accept that wages for summer jobs be reduced by 10 crowns an hour compared to wages paid in 1996. Labour Minister Margareta Winberg has started a nationwide campaign to get employers to open factory doors wider to young people.

- Soft drinks giant Coca-Cola has decided not to run any commercials this year on TV4, Sweden's leading commercial station, saying it is too expensive. Channels TV3, TV5 and ZTV will benefit from Coca-Cola's boycott of TV4.

- A government-appointed commission which was asked to present a way to simplify the system of taxes on advertisements proposes that the tax be abolished entirely. At present daily newspapers pay a four percent surcharge on their ads and other publications pay 11 percent. The situtaion is complicated as ads carried by new media, such as on CDs, are not subject to tax at all.
